item.title: 5 Things to Know About Adam Hamilton, the Pastor Running for Senate in Kansas
item.description:
Adam Hamilton, a pastor, is hoping his moderate message and local recognition could end a nearly century-long U.S. Senate drought for Democrats in Kansas.

He is looking to defeat the Republican incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist who was elected in 2020. The race is close, according to polls, despite the fact that Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

The seat has become an unexpected battleground on a midterm map that has put many Republican strongholds in play amid rising frustrations with President Trump.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Hamilton.

Mr. Hamilton is the founder and pastor of Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, with around 24,000 members in three states. Mr. Hamilton stepped away from the pulpit in June to campaign but has said he plans to keep working as a senior pastor if he is elected. Mr. Marshall has used Mr. Hamilton’s role in the church as an attack line, deriding him as a “megachurch C.E.O.”

Mr. Hamilton is an unusual Democrat, and his candidacy has made for a surprising — and viable — campaign in a ruby-red state. He was registered as a Republican until earlier this year and had considered running as an independent. He has found supporters among moderate Democrats and some Republicans, including two of the state’s former Republican governors. He has criticized the Iran war and pointed to Mr. Marshall and Mr. Trump as reasons that costs are on the rise in Kansas. His campaign has emphasized making health care more accessible, particularly in rural areas, partly by restoring tax credits and reversing Medicare cuts made by the Trump administration.

The competitiveness of the race has been a shock to many. The Cook Political Report updated its assessment of the race this month to a tossup from leaning Republican. Republicans running across the Midwest are grappling with increasing energy prices and the unpopular war in Iran.

Mr. Hamilton is well known in the state and has struck a moderate tone that has appealed to disillusioned supporters of Mr. Trump. Mr. Marshall, meanwhile, is close to Mr. Trump, who campaigned on the first-term senator’s behalf this week. Mr. Trump has grown unpopular in Kansas, where a majority of voters recently said they disapproved of the president, according to a Times/Siena poll.

In the first nine months of the year, Mr. Hamilton raised $13.4 million, about six times as much as Mr. Marshall raised, Federal Election Commission filings show. Mr. Hamilton reported almost $10 million in the third quarter alone, compared with roughly $800,000 for Mr. Marshall. Republicans have funneled cash into the Kansas race: As of Sunday, the G.O.P.’s main super PAC had spent or reserved more than $11.6 million to support Mr. Marshall, whose fund-raising has lagged.

At least a dozen pastors, seminarians or clergy members have run for federal office as Democrats this year, according to Religion News Service. Among them is James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and Texas’ Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, who, like Mr. Hamilton, has stepped away from religious commitments to campaign. Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister who is running for Congress in Iowa, has continued preaching several times a month. Mr. Hamilton, for his part, has described voting as “an act of Christian discipleship.”

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas
item.description:
Ninety-four years ago. That was the last time Kansans elected a Democrat to the Senate. This year’s race is neck and neck, according to polls, and Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, aims to keep his party’s streak going.

But increasing displeasure with President Trump’s economic policies as well as a strong Democratic opponent have Republicans in the state scrambling to shore up Mr. Marshall.

He was elected to the Senate in 2020, after spending decades running an OB-GYN medical practice in rural central Kansas. He comfortably won that election by 11 points.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Marshall’s candidacy.

On Monday night, Mr. Trump stumped for Mr. Marshall near Wichita. The president sought to credit him with being the driving force behind a new pledge to offer $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel fuel prices. Mr. Marshall also campaigned with Vice President JD Vance last month.

During Mr. Trump’s rambling speech on Monday, he invoked an antisemitic trope while defending Mr. Marshall’s aggressive approach to collecting debts as a doctor. Mr. Trump said that Mr. Marshall had been cast as “some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” referring to the Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice,” whose name has become shorthand for antisemitic representations of avarice and usury.

Mr. Marshall has had to tiptoe around his support for some of the Trump administration’s policies. He has criticized its immigration enforcement actions, which have often targeted farm workers. A Times/Siena poll last month found that 55 percent of Kansans disapprove of the way Mr. Trump is handling his job as president, and that half said they thought Mr. Marshall would support Mr. Trump too much.

As elsewhere, the economy is center stage in Kansas. Amid disruptions caused by the war in Iran, Kansas’ agricultural economy has been hit particularly hard by the rising price of diesel, which is used in equipment from combine harvesters to irrigation pumps. Fertilizer costs have skyrocketed as well.

The state’s cattle ranchers were hurt by the Trump administration’s decision earlier this year to allow a flood of cheap beef imports into the United States, which lowered prices for consumers at the expense of domestic producers.

Those challenges added to the woes of farmers and ranchers who were already contending with a drought that has reduced yields of mainstay crops like corn, soybeans and wheat.

Mr. Marshall raised $2.5 million in individual campaign contributions by early October, compared with more than $4 million for Mr. Hamilton.

Since then, millions more have poured into the race on both sides from super PACs and outside donors. Even as Republicans have sought to divert campaign cash from other states to Kansas in recent weeks, Mr. Hamilton has continued to eclipse Mr. Marshall’s fund-raising.

Mr. Marshall, either personally or through his practice, filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, according to a New York Times analysis of Kansas court records. Patients were arrested in 81 of those cases for missing court dates. The unpaid bills ranged from several thousand dollars to as little as $101, and patients were routinely charged an 18 percent annual interest rate.

Mr. Marshall responded to The Times’s investigation last month, calling it “an absolute lie” and telling Fox News that he would “never want anyone to be arrested because of money that they owe myself or the hospital.” He said the lawsuits were a result of “standard practices.”

Of the state’s four living Republican former governors, none have endorsed Mr. Marshall. Two — Bill Graves and Mike Hayden — have endorsed Mr. Hamilton, while the other two, Sam Brownback and Jeff Colyer, have stayed neutral. The current governor of Kansas, Laura Kelly, endorsed her fellow Democrat.

In his endorsement, Mr. Graves wrote that Mr. Marshall had “turned his back” on Kansas and that Mr. Hamilton knew how to “disagree without being disagreeable.” Mr. Hayden’s message was much the same, accusing Mr. Marshall of putting “party and politics ahead of the people.” Regarding the Trump administration’s economic policies, he argued that Mr. Hamilton would be more “willing to stand up and say, ‘This isn’t working.’”

item.title: Clashes Darken Rally in South Carolina as Trump Seeks to Boost Darline Graham
item.description:
More than half a dozen clashes between rallygoers and protesters interrupted President Trump at an appearance in Clemson, S.C., on Wednesday night, where he had traveled to boost the campaign of Senator Darline Graham.

It was not the first Trump rally in recent days marred by protests. But the drumbeat of outbursts, followed by angry reactions by the president and his supporters, showed the deep political divide in the country as the Nov. 3 elections draw near.

Mr. Trump is in the midst of a six-day barnstorm across some the country’s most conservative states, seeking to shore up support among his fans at a time when Republicans are increasingly pessimistic about whether they can retain control of Congress.

South Carolina is among a raft of traditionally Republican strongholds that have become battlegrounds this cycle. Polling in these places shows that Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries for everyday Americans — have threatened the party’s fortunes.

The clashes on Wednesday between protesters, who interrupted Mr. Trump with screams and expletives, and rallygoers who responded with similar aggression, underscored how much is at stake in these midterms for a deeply polarized electorate.

One after the next, security officers escorted the protesters out of the arena, while the president’s fans whooped, jeered and chanted “U.S.A.” Mr. Trump did little to de-escalate the atmosphere.

“They’re terrible people,” he said after hearing one disruption.

“Who’s that guy who threw a punch?” he asked after another, appearing to celebrate when a rallygoer physically confronted a demonstrator.

Mr. Trump had traveled to this livestock facility in the northwest corner of South Carolina to help Ms. Graham at a time when polls show her in an unexpectedly tight race against her Democratic opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews.

The South Carolina governor, Henry McMaster, appointed Ms. Graham over the summer to fill out the remainder of the term of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July. The president then endorsed her for a full six-year term.

His choice of Ms. Graham, who had no prior political experience, in a tough political environment for Republicans has forced the party to pour resources into defending a seat in a state Mr. Trump carried in 2024 by more than 17 points.

On Tuesday, the Cook Political Report shifted the Senate race toward Dr. Andrews for the second time in less than a month, this time from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

The rally showed signs of helping Ms. Graham, who needs to varnish her conservative credentials in a region called the Upstate, where ultraconservative voters were known to be critical of her brother for what they viewed as his soft stance on immigration and history of compromising with Democrats.

Mr. Trump drew a full house to the facility, and the crowd whooped and hollered at his punchlines on immigration and the media with energy reminiscent of his rallies in prior cycles. He invited Ms. Graham, who had spoken earlier in the evening, to join him onstage.

“This area, and most importantly its values, are ingrained in me,” said Ms. Graham, who was raised in the Upstate. “God, family, country.”

Earlier in the night, Senator Tim Scott and Representative Russell Fry, who ran against Ms. Graham in a bitterly fought primary election, vouched for her conservative bona fides.

Mr. Trump’s extensive efforts on behalf of Ms. Graham helped her win the primary election, but not without avoiding a runoff election against Representative Ralph Norman, the vice chair of the hard-line Freedom Caucus. Counties in the Upstate broke for Mr. Norman, who has been at best a reluctant supporter of Ms. Graham’s general election candidacy.

On a podcast episode that aired on Wednesday, Mr. Norman said he would vote for Ms. Graham, but his family would not. Mr. Norman also said he would not do any events with his former opponent — a promise he appeared to keep on Wednesday, when he was nowhere to be found at Clemson.

Mr. Trump spoke for about an hour and a half. At one point, he said he was in a “good mood.” At other moments, he looked into the crowd and saw men with their middle fingers in the air, then watched as security officers escorted them from the hall.

item.title: Judge Restricts D.H.S. Field Operations Aimed at Unearthing Voter Fraud
item.description:
A federal judge in California on Wednesday blocked the Homeland Security Department from carrying out most field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in nine states as part of a broader push to identify noncitizen voters.

The ruling came less than two weeks before the midterm elections. The Trump administration has launched a blitz of operations focused on finding evidence of noncitizen voting or tying up election processes in states where it has dubiously claimed that large numbers of noncitizens are registered to vote.

The ruling covered stops and field interviews being carried out by hundreds of Department of Homeland Security agents assigned to fan out across the country in search of instances of voter fraud, under what the administration has referred to as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative.”

In a concise 19-page ruling, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote that the stops appeared likely to hamper voter engagement and registration by a coalition of local governments and nonprofit groups. As with other initiatives in which the Trump administration has used federal immigration data to infer the citizenship status of people on state voter rolls, she wrote there were already signs that the “target lists” the government had generated contained errors and included naturalized citizens.

The Department of Homeland Security has defended its methods, saying federal officials had used multiple data sources in addition to the public voter data they pulled to further verify the identity of registrants and eliminate false positives.

Judge Martínez-Olguin stopped short of halting field operations. But she barred agents from carrying out interviews that “involve or are likely to involve persons” who agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.” Given the unreliability of federal citizenship data at issue in the case, it was unclear how significantly that would hamper the department’s activities.

The interests of the entities suing, “and the public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation,” she wrote, “far exceed defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens.”

Internal documents introduced in the case indicated that agents were directed to focus on California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Judge Martínez-Olguin, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., wrote that the scope of the operations also raised concerns about voter intimidation. She noted that according to agency memos, the Homeland Security Department “surveils, covertly infiltrates and interrogates the staff of nonprofits and churches conducting voter engagement” and had targeted nearly 150 such nonprofit groupsas of July.

The government had indicated it could target naturalized citizens in instances where data suggested an individual had voted before they were naturalized.

The case arose as the Trump administration has mounted a series of legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections. The efforts have been largely unsuccessful, in part because many of the state and local authorities that administer and supervise elections have refused to comply with demands for access to sensitive voter rolls.

As a result, the federal authorities have compiled their own databases, underpinned by public, commercially available information that they have compared with federal records. The process has led to mistakes in some states, in part because public voter rolls do not include unique identifiers like Social Security numbers. Federal immigration records also sometimes fail to capture changes in citizenship status.

Election authorities in Los Angeles said the Justice Department’s lists of suspected noncitizen voters were so sloppily compiled that they seemed almost “performative” in nature, with thousands of names lacking Social Security numbers and other crucial identifying information. Many of the names, they said, were paired with addresses over which Los Angeles had no jurisdiction.

A spokesman for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office said the list was initially sent on a thumb drive that was unusable because it posed a risk to sensitive voter information, and called the federal demand “a data dump.”

Judge Martínez-Olguin paused her order from taking effect until Friday evening, allowing the government time to appeal. She wrote that order would lift at the end of Election Day, on Nov. 3, “or as otherwise directed by the court.”

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and decades of evidence show that instances of noncitizen voting are exceptionally rare in the United States, far beneath levels that the administration alleges. Scrutiny of claims by the administration that large numbers of noncitizens voted in states like Nevada, for example, have caused the allegations to collapse.

The Homeland Security Department’s operations aimed at finding verified cases of voter fraud comes as the Trump administration has mounted a series of escalating — and largely unsuccessful — legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections.

The administration has particularly singled out states led by Democrats like California, where officials have refused to comply with demands for access to voter rolls. Last week, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles gave local election officials 48 hours to verify the citizenship or segregate the ballots of 20,000 people on a list of potential noncitizens they said had been compiled by the Homeland Security Department.

When California officials said that timeline was impossible to comply with, the Department of Justice filed suit to prevent any ballots sent to those people from being counted.

On Monday, the federal authorities announced they had released from custody 28 immigrants throughout the state who they said were suspected of registering to vote or voting in California elections before becoming naturalized citizens. All had green cards and many denied ever knowingly registering or voting. The group represented a tiny fraction — roughly one in a million — of the roughly 23 million registered voters in the state.

item.title: MAGA Bingo and Questions of Loyalty: 5 Michigan Senate Debate Takeaways
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and former Representative Mike Rogers do not like each other.

The two Senate candidates in Michigan have spent months trying to tear each other down. During their debate on Wednesday, Mr. Rogers questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to the country and sought to tie him to overseas Islamist groups. Dr. El-Sayed characterized Mr. Rogers as bought and paid for by corporate donors and in thrall to President Trump.

And somehow this debate was more civil and substantive than the last time they met, two weeks ago.

Polls show a tight race in a contest that could decide control of the chamber, with Dr. El-Sayed seeking to defend the Michigan seat for Democrats and Mr. Rogers hoping to give Republicans a lift by flipping it.

Here are five takeaways from their second and final debate:

After pushing during the first debate to place Dr. El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and family history at the center of the campaign, Mr. Rogers laid off just a little. He did not mention his opponent’s mother this time around.

Instead, he sought to tie Dr. El-Sayed, an Egyptian American, to the Muslim Brotherhood, a movement founded in Egypt nearly a century ago.

“If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Mr. Rogers asked.

Mr. Rogers somewhat clumsily suggested that Dr. El-Sayed wanted to defund the police not only in the United States, but also in Egypt — because of an open letter he signed in 2012. The letter called on Mohamed Morsi, a member of the Muslim Brotherhood who won Egypt’s first competitive presidential election, to “purge” police officials who had been loyal to the previous autocratic government.

Mr. Morsi was removed from power a year later in a military takeover.

Dr. El-Sayed asked for extra time to deliver a fuller response and then gave a clear declaration of his loyalty to the United States.

“It’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike,” Dr. El-Sayed responded. “I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray. And the question that you would ask, that I think is actually really quite shameful as somebody who’s actually served under that Constitution, it is shameful, shameful.”

Dr. El-Sayed’s debate strategy was clear from the start: He wanted to tether Mr. Rogers to Mr. Trump and not allow his Senate rival to create any political distance from the unpopular president.

Dr. El-Sayed made a case that Mr. Trump, and by extension Mr. Rogers, was responsible for policies that have driven up the costs of fuel, groceries and other daily needs. He invited viewers to play “MAGA bingo,” in a lighthearted attempt to head off words or phrases Mr. Rogers might use to attack him. And he noted times when Mr. Rogers dodged questions about White House policy or his connections to Mr. Trump.

“The thing about MAGA is, whenever they’re talking, they are trying to distract you,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “Just remember: When they’re distracting you, they’re also trying to pick your pocket. It’s a form of corporatized bribery.”

Mr. Rogers made a pitch to the Democratic voters who opposed Dr. El-Sayed in the party’s hard-fought Senate primary race in August.

He made an explicit appeal to voters who backed Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate Democrat, particularly Black voters and Jews. Anger among some Jewish Michiganders about Dr. El-Sayed’s left-wing opposition to Israel has for months worried Democrats who want him to win.

But Mr. Rogers’s appeal to Black voters could also be significant in the general election. Black voters make up roughly 12 percent of the Michigan electorate, while Jewish voters make up less than 2 percent. Mr. Rogers cited his work on housing in Detroit and pointed to what he described as his campaign’s success with Black voters.

“We’re doing well with African Americans in the city of Detroit, in Pontiac, in Flint,” Mr. Rogers said.

A key part of Dr. El-Sayed’s electoral strategy is to build a voting coalition that looks different from how Democrats have won in Michigan in the past.

He may do worse with moderate Democrats in the Detroit suburbs, but he is banking on improving on his party’s performance in rural areas that have swung toward Republicans during the Trump years.

On Wednesday, Dr. El-Sayed pointed to his crowds during his trip last week to Michigan’s conservative Upper Peninsula. There, he said, voters brought the same concerns about high costs as people he had met elsewhere in the state.

“We had 500 people in Iron Mountain, 600 in Escanaba, 1,300 in Marquette, all coming together around a vision for an America where it just shouldn’t be this hard,” he said.

Mr. Rogers was keen to invoke his wife, which male politicians often do to try to soften their own image.

At the beginning of the debate, Mr. Rogers said “my wife and I” had decided to run for the Senate, as if she were on the ballot with him.

Later, he seemed to imply that his wife, Kristi Rogers, who worked in Iraq as a civilian employee of the Defense Department during the Iraq war, had served in the military, as he and other members of his family did.

“I wore the uniform of the United States proudly, as my son did, my wife served, my brother served, my father served,” Mr. Rogers said.

A Rogers campaign spokeswoman, Abby Ronson, said after the debate that Ms. Rogers had “felt called to serve our great country after 9/11, and we thank her for answering the call to protect Americans.”

item.title: Farmers, Health Care and Highways: 5 Takeaways from the Kansas Senate Debate
item.description:
Once upon a time, the Kansas Senate race was expected to be a sleepy affair, one where Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, would cruise to re-election.

Then came Adam Hamilton.

In a matter of months, Mr. Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, has turned the deep red state into one of the most unexpected battlegrounds of the midterms, putting Mr. Marshall on the defensive in a contentious campaign that has pumped the airwaves full of attack ads.

So the most surprising thing about Wednesday night’s Senate debate might just have been how civil it was.

The moderator, John Holt of Fox4 in Kansas City, skillfully dispensed with the main attacks of the campaign in its opening minutes and pushed the two men instead to tangle over substance. They stuck to his rules and — no doubt unintentionally — even presented a unified sartorial front, wearing matching dark suits and silvery ties.

And both candidates tried to use their time onstage to transform the race into a referendum on unpopular national figures: President Trump and Senator Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader.

Here are five takeaways from the night.

No one has more practice at extemporaneous talking than a megachurch pastor.

Mr. Hamilton, who founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, is comfortable delivering sermons and speaking on long podcasts. That showed, as he deftly navigated a lightning-speed debate that veered from foreign policy to farming to artificial intelligence, creating a stark contrast with Mr. Marshall, who spoke haltingly and sometimes tripped over his words.

Mr. Hamilton blamed Mr. Marshall for what he framed as the excesses of the Trump administration — including record diesel prices and immigration raids in farm country — while seeking to present himself as an independent-minded Democrat who has steered clear of his own party’s more extreme positions.

He spoke sparingly about his faith, but used his status as a political newcomer to separate himself from the national party, as when Mr. Marshall sought to connect him to former President Barack Obama’s immigration policies.

“You were pointing at me as though I developed these policies,” Mr. Hamilton said. “I just want to remind you, I’ve been a pastor for the last 38 years. I have not been a senator. I didn’t develop policies with President Obama or anyone else.”

Mr. Holt, the moderator, lobbed detailed questions at the candidates and pressed repeatedly when they tried to sidestep them. At times, Mr. Hamilton answered with candor: He just wasn’t sure.

At one point, Mr. Holt asked both candidates where, exactly, they would draw the line on subsidies for farmers — a delicate question in a year when farmers are facing strong economic headwinds, some of which have been exacerbated by the Trump administration.

Mr. Marshall defended the subsidies.

Mr. Hamilton, who has said on the campaign trail that he doesn’t want to come up with “bogus” answers, said: “I don’t really have an answer to that. I can only say this: that we do need to be able to help our farmers. Our farmers need support.”

He said he would raise the cap on Social Security, but he wasn’t sure to what level. And he said he wasn’t sure what federal regulations he would support on artificial intelligence, in part because, he said, no one in Congress fully understands its dangers.

Mr. Marshall moved to highlight Mr. Hamilton’s inexperience, including once after an exchange over Israel — a country Mr. Hamilton said he had visited 12 times.

For “a novice even to start making national security policy without all the details, I think it’s really hard to do that,” Mr. Marshall said.

Republican candidates running in more traditional battleground states have attempted to distance themselves from President Trump and his unpopular policies, including the Iran war and tariffs. But not Mr. Marshall.

The senator offered a vocal defense of the president, saying he had fulfilled some of his central promises to voters. Mr. Trump, said Mr. Marshall, had strengthened the nation’s military, secured the borders and passed a sweeping tax cut.

His comments were part of an effort to remind Republican voters, including those frustrated by high gas prices and inflation, what they liked about the president. “If you want the Trump agenda to continue,” he said. “you need to come out, because we delivered on those things.”

Two years ago, Mr. Trump won Kansas by 16 points. To win this year, Mr. Marshall must persuade those voters to stick with Republicans, rather than stay home or cross party lines and vote for Mr. Hamilton.

“We need the Trump voters to come out,” he said.

With Mr. Trump facing record low approval ratings, Mr. Marshall attempted to energize Kansas Republicans by reminding them of a figure they like even less: Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader in the Senate.

Again and again, Mr. Marshall warned that electing Mr. Hamilton would award control of the Senate to Democrats and Mr. Schumer. “This guy’s funded by Chuck Schumer,” he said. “He’ll be beholden to Chuck Schumer forever, and that’s why we have to keep me in that Senate seat.”

The repeated invocation of Mr. Schumer’s name was part of an effort by Mr. Marshall to nationalize the race, turning it into a referendum — not on Mr. Trump but on which party controls the Senate. While Mr. Trump is unpopular, Democrats also have plenty of detractors in this red state.

Mr. Hamilton has said he would not support Mr. Schumer as the head of the party in the Senate, arguing that Democrats need fresh leadership. In the debate, he tried to distance himself from national Democrats, calling former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s immigration policy a “disaster” and saying he does not agree with the “socialist party.”

“If I’m elected, as a moderate or independent-minded Democrat, I’m going to work across the aisle,” he said.

As the Kansas Senate race has grown more competitive, it has also become far more contentious.

The debate opened with both candidates being pressed on issues on which they have faced personal criticism. Mr. Marshall defended his aggressive debt collection practices as an obstetrician-gynecologist. Mr. Hamilton attempted to distance himself from an incident of child sex abuse at a church retreat two decades ago.

But they were also pressed on a range of substantive policy questions, including weapons support for Israel, immigration reform and health insurance. Mr. Hamilton hammered Mr. Marshall for backing unpopular policies of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran and tariffs.

For his part, Mr. Marshall attempted to link his opponent to unpopular positions held by some in his party, including support for trans girls playing women’s sports. (Mr. Hamilton said he would not want his 12-year-old granddaughter competing against biological men or boys, saying, “it’s not a fair fight.”)

But not every question was quite as serious.

In a Kansas twist, the moderator asked each candidate to select his favorite stretch of highway in the state.

Mr. Marshall chose Interstate 77 between Manhattan and Cassoday. Mr. Hamilton chose Interstate 35 through the Flint Hills. “One of the most beautiful places on God’s green earth,” he said.

item.title: Four Takeaways From the Debate for Wisconsin Governor
item.description:
Representative Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin and David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, faced off on Wednesday over taxes, abortion and the influence of billionaires in a televised debate, their first and only one before the November election.

In Wisconsin, where statewide races are often decided by razor-thin margins, the debate was a crucial opportunity for Mr. Crowley to introduce himself to voters and for Mr. Tiffany to woo independents hesitant about his close ties with President Trump.

Polls show the candidates in a tight race less than two weeks from Election Day. Democrats hope to keep the governor’s mansion in their party’s hands — and possibly flip control of both the State Senate and the Assembly from Republicans to Democrats.

Here are four takeaways from Wednesday night’s debate, which was held at Marquette University in Milwaukee and hosted by a local news station, WISN 12.

Early in the debate, Mr. Tiffany, who was endorsed by President Trump, did not directly answer when asked how voters could trust him to represent their interests when he is so closely aligned with the president.

Mr. Tiffany is one of the most conservative members of Congress, known for his strong support for gun rights and lowering taxes and his opposition to using taxpayer money for abortions.

“As a lifelong resident, I will make sure that we are going to do what’s right for Wisconsin,” Mr. Tiffany said, before pivoting to wish his wife a happy anniversary and reminiscing about their first date at the Thirsty Whale, a restaurant in Minocqua, Wis.

He did not mention Mr. Trump.

But Mr. Crowley did — frequently. He said that Mr. Tiffany was part of the Trump agenda in Washington, which he said includes tariffs, “endless wars” and high gas prices.

The candidates sparred over how to improve the economy and bring in more revenue to Wisconsin, where families have pointed to affordability as one of the issues driving the governor’s race.

Mr. Tiffany said that he would support building more data centers under certain conditions: no more state subsidies, no increase in utility rates and a requirement that local communities be included in the decision-making process. He also insisted that no data centers be built “on our beautiful farmland here in Wisconsin,” a stipulation that seemed to open the door for building on former industrial sites.

Mr. Crowley, whom Mr. Tiffany has called “Data Center David” on the campaign trial, said that he supports a “pause” in data centers so that their environmental impact can be considered.

Both candidates were enthusiastic about legalizing marijuana — but with conditions.

Wisconsin, where marijuana is illegal, is now an outlier in the region. That has not stopped Wisconsin residents from driving into Minnesota, Michigan and Illinois and buying it in those states.

While Mr. Tiffany said he favored legalizing medical marijuana, Mr. Crowley said he supported full legalization of recreational sales as well.

“This is an opportunity that we’re missing out on as a state,” he said. Making a reference to Gov. J.B. Pritzker of neighboring Illinois, he added: “Look, Governor Pritzker literally thanked Wisconsin residents because they have made $30 million in sales tax collection just from Wisconsin residents.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Crowley has tried to draw attention to his support for abortion rights, in contrast to Mr. Tiffany, who has cosponsored a bill in Congress that would ban abortion after about six weeks of pregnancy.

Wisconsin currently bans abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy and requires an ultrasound and a 24-hour waiting period before an abortion can be performed. About two-thirds of Wisconsin residents say that abortion should be legal in most or all cases, polls show.

On Wednesday, Mr. Crowley dodged the question when asked if he would sign a law that would expand access to abortion with no limits.

“These are decisions that need to be made between a patient and a health care provider,” he said.

Mr. Tiffany said that he had listened to feedback from constituents on the campaign trail who had urged him to find a “common ground.” In response to a question from the moderators, he said he would not sign a hypothetical bill that would ban abortion after fetal cardiac activity could be detected.

Wisconsin is not overflowing with billionaires. But Mr. Crowley did his best to tie them to Mr. Tiffany, part of a continued line of attack connecting Mr. Tiffany to the rich and powerful in Washington.

“He’s working for the billionaires,” Mr. Crowley said. “He’s going to do anything and everything that they tell him to do because that’s who he’s been in the pockets of.”

At one point, Mr. Tiffany seemed fed up with the word.

“He’s misrepresenting our positions, and he’s over there ranting constantly about billionaires,” he said.

For his part, Mr. Tiffany tried to fuse Mr. Crowley’s positions as a Democrat with those of the opponent he defeated in the primary, Francesca Hong, who is a democratic socialist.

“He said, ‘There’s very little difference between me and Francesca Hong,’” he said. “That sounds like a socialist to me.”

Despite repeated pressing by the moderators, Matt Smith and Gerron Jordan, both candidates avoided specifics about how much they would raise or lower property and income taxes and how they would balance the state budget while also fulfilling pledges to make life more affordable for Wisconsin residents.
